title: Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu opening
hook: Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu opening

segments.voice: Last week ended on the chart of Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu, where every feeling has a place. A new week, and Rupa stops charting and starts defining.

Take four in a recording booth. The singer has every note of the devotional song. The producer leans on the talkback button. Lovely, he says. But who's it for? She stops to think. The label, a little. Her mother, who'll cry at the release. The comments she'll read later. And somewhere under the pile, the one the song is actually addressed to. She sings it again. Something has changed, and nobody in the room could say what. Rupa Goswami, a student of Chaitanya, wrote a whole ocean of a book on devotion, and early on he tries to say exactly what.
screen: `TAKE FOUR IN THE BOOTH.` → `LOVELY. BUT WHO'S IT FOR?` → `SOMETHING CHANGED. WHAT?`

segments.voice: He does it in a single verse, and half of it is about what to leave out. In paraphrase: the highest bhakti is turning toward Krishna, again and again, in a way he would welcome. It's empty of desire for anything else, and it isn't covered over by knowledge, ritual work and the like. Start with the center. Rupa's word is anushilana, a steady cultivating, the way someone tends a garden every morning. Bhakti here isn't a mood that visits once. It's done, and done again. Then the manner: favorably, the way a friend turns toward a friend. Then the two things it isn't. It isn't mixed with other wants. And it isn't covered by jnana or karma, knowledge or duty. Covered is the key word. Knowledge and duty can be there in a devotee's life. They just don't sit on top of the love and smother it. That's what changed in the booth. The label and the comments slid off the top, and the song was for the one it was written to. Right after, Rupa quotes an older text, the Narada Pancharatra, for a second definition. In paraphrase: bhakti is serving the lord of the senses with the senses. So the eyes, the hands and the singing voice aren't in the way. They're the instruments.
screen: `TURNING TO KRISHNA, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `IN A WAY HE WOULD WELCOME.` · `NO OTHER WANTING, NOTHING ON TOP.` · then, large: `THE SENSES SERVE THE LORD OF THE SENSES.`

segments.voice: If there's paper and a pen near you, write down one thing you do often: a song, a meal you cook, a message to a friend. Under it, write honestly who it's for, every name on the pile. Then sit with the page and let your eyes rest on the last name, the one at the bottom.
Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu: the ocean of devotion's nectar. It opens by defining the highest bhakti: turning to Krishna gladly, wanting nothing else, nothing laid on top.
screen: `RUPA GOSWAMI'S BHAKTI RASAMRITA SINDHU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Keep this one: Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu opening, where nothing is laid over the love. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1667 COUNTS.` → `RUPA'S OCEAN · 3 OF 7.` → `TOMORROW: WHY SHRUG AT LIBERATION?`

howItsDone: In Gaudiya Vaishnava communities, Rupa Goswami's book is studied with a teacher, and its definition of the highest bhakti is used to look honestly at why one serves.

fork.setup: a friend leads the song at a temple program. she knows the meaning of every word and keeps a careful schedule. by Rupa's definition, what would make it the highest bhakti?
options: nothing else wanted, and the study and schedule not smothering the love.
dropping the study and the schedule, so only the feeling is left.
knowing more than anyone else in the room about the song.
fork.reveal: Rupa doesn't ask her to give up knowledge or duty. The highest bhakti is turning to Krishna gladly, with nothing else wanted and nothing laid on top.

original.note: Sanskrit: the ocean (sindhu) of the nectar (amrita) of bhakti's taste (rasa), the name of Rupa Goswami's book.

trapdoor: what you thought: pure devotion means giving up thinking and doing.
what it means: a steady, welcoming turning toward Krishna, with nothing else wanted and nothing laid on top.
what a scholar hears: Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu 1.1.11, with the Narada Pancharatra quoted just after it.
recall: action, done without grasping at its fruit

chat.says: nani signed me up to lead a bhajan at the senior send-off. should i learn what every word means first?
options: learn them if you like. just don't let the studying sit on top of the song.
skip it. Rupa says real devotion drops study and thinking altogether.
yes. the bhajan only counts once you understand every single word.
chat.meaning: Rupa's highest bhakti isn't covered by knowledge or duty. Study can stay; it just can't smother the love the song is for.

Rupa Goswami.meaning: a follower of Chaitanya who wrote the Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu

anushilana.meaning: steady cultivating, like tending a garden

Narada Pancharatra.meaning: an older devotional text Rupa quotes for a second definition

Chaitanya.meaning: the singer of Krishna's names whom Rupa followed

sources.ref: Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu 1.1.11 (the highest bhakti: favorable cultivation of Krishna, empty of other desires, not covered by knowledge, ritual work and the like)
Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu 1.1.12, quoting the Narada Pancharatra (serving the lord of the senses with the senses, freed from labels, pure by being for him)

notes: Rupa Goswami block, day 3 of 7 (1665–1671): the definition (1.1.11–12). Verse numbers follow the common Gaudiya numbering; confirm 1.1.11 and 1.1.12 and the paraphrases.
'Anushilana' glossed as steady cultivating; Jiva Goswami's commentary reads it as activity of body, speech and mind. Confirm the garden image is fair.
